unit.unitOverview: The passive is one form applied across every tense you have, so learning it once gives you nine or ten new structures at no extra cost. It is also the most criticised construction in English, usually unfairly — it does three jobs nothing else does, and one job it should not be doing. This unit covers the mechanism, the four legitimate reasons to use it, and the fourth reason, which is hiding who acted.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns and they are one pattern in four tenses.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is the whole mechanism; cards 2 to 4 apply it.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a findings report and the letter it produced.
Do the Practice. Practice 4 is the diagnostic — should this be passive at all?
Record yourself describing a process and then a decision.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
The passive is efficient to learn, because it is one mechanism applied to every tense you already have. Learn the mechanism once and you get the whole set.
The mechanism is: be, in whatever tense you want, plus the past participle.
That is all of it. The tense lives in be, and the participle never changes.
Active: They check the trolleys.
Passive: The trolleys are checked.
Active: They checked the trolleys.
Passive: The trolleys were checked.
Same participle both times — checked. Only be moved.
So the full set is:
Present simple: is checked, are checked.
Past simple: was checked, were checked.
Present continuous: is being checked.
Past continuous: was being checked.
Present perfect: has been checked, have been checked.
Past perfect: had been checked.
Future: will be checked.
Modals: must be checked, should be checked, can be checked, might have been checked.
Ten structures from one rule, and you already know every tense involved.
Notice what happened to the sentence. The object of the active sentence — the trolleys — has become the subject of the passive one. And the person doing it has disappeared.
If you want to put them back, use by. The trolleys are checked by the supervisor.
But here is the important fact about by, and it surprises people. In real English, the by phrase is omitted about eighty per cent of the time. The passive is mostly used precisely because you do not want to name the agent, or because naming them is unnecessary.
Which brings us to the real question of this unit: when should you use it?
There are four reasons, and three of them are good.
Reason one: the agent is unknown. The window was broken overnight. You do not know who broke it. There is no active version available.
Reason two: the agent is obvious and saying it would be noise. The suspect was arrested. Obviously by the police. My car was stolen. Obviously by a thief. Adding by the police adds nothing.
Reason three, and this is the biggest one: the thing is more important than the person doing it. This is why the passive dominates in descriptions of processes, procedures and rules.
The samples are collected each morning and sent to the laboratory. Who collects them is not the point; the process is the point. Rewriting that actively — a technician collects the samples — forces a person into a sentence that was about a system.
This is also why instructions and technical writing are full of it. The unit must be switched off before cleaning. The relevant thing is the unit and the rule, not who is holding the cloth.
Reason four is the one that gets the passive its bad name: hiding the agent.
Mistakes were made. A decision was taken. Your application has been rejected.
Every one of those is grammatically fine and every one of them removes a person who exists and is known.
Notice that this is the same move as the abstract nouns in Unit 8, and the two are usually found together. There has been a reduction in staffing levels combines both — a nominalisation and no agent, in eight words.
So the passive is not a bad construction. It is a tool with a legitimate function that can also be used to avoid responsibility, and the skill is telling the two apart.
The test I would give you is a question: is the agent unknown, obvious, or irrelevant?
If yes to any of those, the passive is correct and probably better than the active.
If no — if the agent is known, specific and relevant — then ask why they are not in the sentence. Sometimes there is a good reason. Often there is not.
One more practical thing, about a form that trips people up.
Some verbs take two objects, and both can become the subject of a passive.
They gave me the form. That can become I was given the form, or the form was given to me.
English strongly prefers the first — the person, not the thing. I was given, I was told, I was sent, I was offered, I was asked. Those are extremely common and worth having.
And finally, a warning about the participle. The passive uses the third form, not the past simple. The trolleys were checked is fine because checked is both. But the door was broke is wrong — it is was broken. The report was wrote is wrong — it is was written.
So the twenty irregular verbs from Level 1 Unit 14 and their third column from Unit 3 of this level come back here, and this is where getting them wrong is most visible.
Go to Patterns.

readings.passageScript:
The passive is unusually efficient to learn, because it is a single mechanism applied to tenses you already have.
The mechanism: be, in whatever tense you want, plus the past participle.
The tense lives in be. The participle never changes.
They check the trolleys becomes the trolleys are checked.
They checked the trolleys becomes the trolleys were checked.
Same participle. Only be moved.
So the whole set comes for free:
is checked, are checked — present simple.
was checked, were checked — past simple.
is being checked — present continuous.
was being checked — past continuous.
has been checked — present perfect.
had been checked — past perfect.
will be checked — future.
must be checked, should be checked, can be checked — modals.
might have been checked — modal plus perfect.
Ten structures, one rule.
Two things happened when the sentence changed.
The object of the active sentence became the subject of the passive one. The trolleys were the thing being checked; now they are what the sentence is about.
And the person doing it disappeared. You can put them back with by — the trolleys are checked by the supervisor — but in real English the by phrase is left out about eighty per cent of the time. That is not laziness. Most passives exist precisely because the agent is unknown, obvious or beside the point.
One warning, and it is where errors are most visible.
The passive uses the past participle — the third form — not the past simple.
The trolleys were checked is safe, because checked is both forms.
The door was broke is wrong. It is was broken.
The report was wrote is wrong. It is was written.
So the third column you built in Unit 3 of this level comes back here, and this is where getting it wrong is hardest to miss.

readings.title: Four Reasons, and One of Them Is Bad
readings.passageScript:
The passive is the most criticised construction in English and most of the criticism is misplaced. It does three jobs that nothing else does, and one job it should not be doing.
Reason one: the agent is unknown. The window was broken overnight. Nobody knows who broke it, and there is no active sentence available to write instead.
Reason two: the agent is obvious, and naming it would be noise. The suspect was arrested. By the police, evidently. My car was stolen. By a thief. Adding the agent adds nothing and makes the sentence worse.
Reason three, and this is the largest: the thing matters more than the person doing it.
The samples are collected each morning and sent to the laboratory.
Who collects them is not the subject. The process is the subject. Rewriting it actively — a technician collects the samples and a driver takes them to the laboratory — forces two people into a sentence that was never about people, and the reader now has to hold them.
This is why the passive dominates in procedures, instructions, technical writing and rules. The unit must be switched off before cleaning. The relevant things are the unit and the requirement, not who is holding the cloth.
Reason four is the one that earned the bad reputation: hiding a known agent.
Mistakes were made. A decision was taken. Your application has been rejected. Staff levels have been reduced.
Every one is grammatically correct. Every one removes a person who exists, is known, and is relevant.
And notice this is the same move as the abstract nouns in Unit 8. The two travel together, because both remove agents. There has been a reduction in staffing levels does it twice in eight words — a nominalisation and a passive-like construction, and not a person in sight.
So the test is a question, and it is short.
Is the agent unknown, obvious, or irrelevant?
If yes to any, the passive is right and often better than the active.
If no — if the agent is known, specific and relevant — ask why they are not in the sentence. Sometimes the answer is good. Often it is that somebody preferred not to say.

readings.setting: An extract from an internal findings report, and the letter sent to the person concerned.
readings.passageScript:
FINDINGS - extract

  4.1  The loading was inspected on 14
       March by D. Okonkwo, Supervisor.

  4.2  Three trolleys were found to be
       loaded above the marked line.

  4.3  The loading sheet had not been
       completed since 9 March.

  4.4  Ms Adeyemi confirmed that she had
       been allocated to Bay 3 for the
       whole of that week and had not
       been asked to cover Bay 2.

  4.5  No instruction to cover Bay 2 was
       issued by the shift manager.

  4.6  A breach of procedure 7.1 is
       recorded. Responsibility is
       attributed to the shift manager.

-----------------------------------------

  LETTER SENT TO MS ADEYEMI

  Dear Ms Adeyemi,

  Following a review of loading practice
  on Bay 2, it has been found that
  procedure 7.1 was not followed during
  the week commencing 9 March.

  The loading sheet had not been
  completed and three trolleys were
  found to be overloaded.

  It has been decided that a written
  reminder will be issued to all
  warehouse staff.

  This matter is now considered closed.

grammar.title: The passive: the mechanism
grammar.explanation: One rule that applies to every tense you already have. Learn it once and ten structures come with it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
BE + PAST PARTICIPLE
  the tense lives in BE.
  the participle NEVER changes.

  They check the trolleys.
  -> The trolleys ARE CHECKED.
  They checked the trolleys.
  -> The trolleys WERE CHECKED.

THE WHOLE SET
  present     is / are checked
  past        was / were checked
  pres cont   is being checked
  past cont   was being checked
  pres perf   has / have been checked
  past perf   had been checked
  future      will be checked
  modal       must / should / can be checked
  modal perf  might have been checked

WHAT MOVED
  the OBJECT became the SUBJECT.
  the agent DISAPPEARED.
  put it back with BY - but in real
  English BY is omitted about 80% of
  the time.

USE THE THIRD FORM, NOT THE PAST
  was broke   X   -> was BROKEN
  was wrote   X   -> was WRITTEN
  (checked is safe: both forms match)
grammar.workedExample:
Turn they checked the trolleys on Tuesday into the passive.
1. Find the object of the active sentence: the trolleys. That becomes the subject.
2. Find the tense: past simple. So be goes into the past simple: were, because trolleys is plural.
3. Add the past participle: checked.
4. Result: The trolleys were checked on Tuesday.
5. Do you need the agent? They is vague and adds nothing, so leave it out. That is the normal case.
Now the same sentence with a modal. They must check the trolleys.
1. The modal stays where it is: must.
2. After a modal, be is in its plain form: must be.
3. Add the participle: must be checked.
4. Result: The trolleys must be checked.
And one with an irregular verb. They wrote the report.
1. Past simple, singular subject: was.
2. The participle of write is written, not wrote.
3. Result: The report was written.
grammar.commonMistake: Using the past simple instead of the past participle — was broke, was wrote, was took. With regular verbs the two forms are identical so the error never appears; with irregular verbs it is highly visible. The other error is adding a by phrase that carries no information: the trolleys were checked by somebody, by them, by people.
grammar.memoryTip: Be plus the third form. The tense lives in be.
grammar.practice:
Make each one passive. Leave out the agent unless it adds something.
1. They check the trolleys.
2. They checked the trolleys on Tuesday.
3. Somebody broke the door.
4. She wrote the report.
5. They must check the trolleys.
6. They have inspected the site.
grammar.answerKey:
1. The trolleys are checked.
2. The trolleys were checked on Tuesday.
3. The door was broken.
4. The report was written. (or: by her — but only if who wrote it matters)
5. The trolleys must be checked.
6. The site has been inspected.
Numbers 3 and 4 use the third form — broken and written, not broke and wrote. That is where the visible errors happen.
None of these needs a by phrase. In 1, 2, 5 and 6 the agent is either unknown or beside the point, which is the normal situation.
In 5, be stays in its plain form after must, and the participle does not change at all.

grammar.title: The passive with modals and the perfect
grammar.explanation: No new rule. The same mechanism with be in a different tense, and this is where the structures learners find most useful in real writing appear.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
AFTER A MODAL, BE IS PLAIN
  must be checked
  should be checked
  can be checked
  may be suspended
  has to be dismantled

THE PERFECT: HAS / HAVE / HAD BEEN
  has been checked
  have been distributed
  had been completed

MODAL + PERFECT: MODAL + HAVE BEEN
  might have been checked
  should have been reported
  could have been prevented

THE CONTINUOUS: BE + BEING + PARTICIPLE
  is being installed
  was being investigated

  ^ being is what makes it continuous.
    Without it: is installed = a rule.
    With it: is being installed = now.

NEGATIVES GO AFTER THE FIRST WORD
  has NOT been verified
  must NOT be moved
  could NOT have been prevented

TWO PASSIVES IN ONE SENTENCE
  "The container must be sealed before
   it is moved."
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say a rule: somebody has to inspect every unit before it goes out.
1. The rule is about the units, not about who inspects them, so the passive is right.
2. Obligation takes must or has to. Choose must.
3. After a modal, be is plain: must be.
4. Add the participle: must be inspected.
5. Result: Every unit must be inspected before dispatch.
Now a perfect passive. You want to say the figures have not been checked.
1. Present perfect passive is has or have been plus the participle.
2. Figures is plural: have been.
3. The negative goes after the first word: have not been.
4. Result: The figures have not been verified.
And a continuous passive. The system is being installed right now.
1. Present continuous passive is is or are, plus being, plus the participle.
2. Result: The system is being installed.
3. Compare it without being: the system is installed. That is a standing fact or a rule, not something happening this week. Being is doing the whole job.
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving out being in the continuous passive, which turns something happening now into a general statement — the system is installed means it is in place, not that work is under way. The other error is putting the participle straight after a modal without be: it must checked. And forgetting that after a modal, be never inflects — must be, never must is.
grammar.memoryTip: After a modal, be is plain. Being is what makes it continuous.
grammar.practice:
Write the passive.
1. Somebody must inspect every unit. (rule)
2. Nobody has verified the figures.
3. They are installing the system this week.
4. Somebody should have reported it.
5. Nobody could have prevented it.
6. They were investigating the incident at the time.
7. Nobody has audited the accounts this year.
8. Somebody has to dismantle it before it is moved.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Every unit must be inspected.
2. The figures have not been verified.
3. The system is being installed this week.
4. It should have been reported.
5. It could not have been prevented.
6. The incident was being investigated at the time.
7. The accounts have not been audited this year.
8. It has to be dismantled before it is moved.
Numbers 3 and 6 contain being, which is what makes them continuous. Without it, number 3 would mean the system is in place.
Numbers 4 and 5 are modal perfect passives — modal, then have been, then the participle. They are common in reports and worth drilling.
Number 8 has two passives sharing one sentence: has to be dismantled and is moved.

grammar.title: The passive in a process, and the two-object passive
grammar.explanation: The largest legitimate use of the passive, and one form that catches learners: verbs with two objects can be made passive two ways, and English prefers one of them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
PROCESSES ARE WRITTEN IN THE PASSIVE
  because the thing matters more than
  the person.

  "The samples are collected each morning
   and sent to the laboratory. They are
   logged on arrival and stored below
   five degrees."

  Four passives, no people, and the
  reader follows the process rather than
  a cast of staff.

  The active version forces people in:
  "A technician collects the samples and
   a driver takes them..."
  ^ now the reader has to hold two people
    who are not the point.

TWO-OBJECT VERBS - TWO PASSIVES
  "They gave me the form."

  -> I was given the form.        preferred
  -> The form was given to me.    correct

  English prefers the PERSON as subject.

VERY COMMON, WORTH HAVING:
  I was given / told / sent / offered /
  asked / shown / paid / promised

VERBS THAT WORK THIS WAY
  give, tell, send, offer, ask, show,
  pay, promise, teach, lend
grammar.workedExample:
You are describing what happens to a delivery.
1. Ask whether the people matter. A delivery process is about the goods and the steps, not about who performs each one.
2. So use the passive throughout and leave the agents out.
3. Deliveries are booked in on arrival. The paperwork is checked against the order. Any damaged items are recorded and set aside. The rest is allocated to a bay and logged.
4. Five passives, no people, and the reader can follow the sequence.
Now the two-object case. Somebody gave you a form.
1. Give has two objects: me and the form.
2. Either can become the subject: I was given the form, or the form was given to me.
3. English prefers the person: I was given the form.
4. The same pattern gives you I was told, I was sent, I was offered, I was asked — all very common and all built the same way.
Notice that the second version needs to before the person, and the first does not.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing a process in the active because active is supposedly clearer, which forces invented people into every step. The other error is the two-object passive: the form was given me, missing the to. If the thing is the subject, the person needs to — the form was given to me.
grammar.memoryTip: Processes take the passive. With two objects, put the person first.
grammar.practice:
Write the passive.
1. Describe a process in four sentences, all passive, with no people.
2. They gave me the form. (person first)
3. They gave me the form. (thing first)
4. They told us nothing.
5. They sent her the wrong part.
6. They offered him a different date.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Model: Deliveries are booked in on arrival. The paperwork is checked against the order. Damaged items are recorded and set aside. Everything else is allocated to a bay and logged.
2. I was given the form.
3. The form was given to me.
4. We were told nothing.
5. She was sent the wrong part.
6. He was offered a different date.
Numbers 2 and 3 are the same event two ways, and 2 is what English prefers. Notice 3 needs to before me and 2 does not.
Numbers 4, 5 and 6 all put the person first, which is why they sound natural. The alternatives — nothing was told to us, the wrong part was sent to her — are grammatical and much less usual.
In number 1, check that no person appears anywhere. If one crept in, the sentence was probably about them rather than about the process.

grammar.title: When the passive is hiding somebody
grammar.explanation: The fourth reason, and the one that gives the passive its reputation. The construction is not the problem; using it where the agent is known, specific and relevant is.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE TEST - one question
  Is the agent UNKNOWN, OBVIOUS,
  or IRRELEVANT?

  YES to any -> the passive is right,
     and often better than the active.

  NO -> the agent is known, specific and
     relevant. Ask why they are not in
     the sentence.

LEGITIMATE
  The window was broken overnight.
     unknown
  The suspect was arrested.
     obvious
  Samples are stored below five degrees.
     irrelevant - it is a rule

HIDING
  Mistakes were made.
  A decision was taken.
  Your application has been rejected.
  Staff levels have been reduced.
  It has been decided that...

  ^ every agent here is KNOWN.

IT TRAVELS WITH UNIT 8's ABSTRACT NOUNS
  "There has been a reduction in
   staffing levels."
  ^ nominalisation AND no agent,
    in eight words.

RESTORING THE AGENT
  ask: who did this? Then put them back
  and see whether the sentence still
  says the same thing.
grammar.workedExample:
You read: it has been decided that a written reminder will be issued to all warehouse staff.
1. Count the passives. Two: has been decided, will be issued.
2. Apply the test to the first. Is the agent unknown? No — somebody decided. Obvious? No. Irrelevant? No — who decided is exactly what a reader would want to know.
3. So this passive is hiding a known agent.
4. Restore it and see what changes: The shift manager has decided that a written reminder will be issued.
5. Now the sentence names somebody who can be asked about it, which the original carefully did not.
Now one that passes. Samples are stored below five degrees.
1. Is the agent relevant? No — this is a rule about samples, and it applies to whoever handles them.
2. Naming somebody would make it worse: a technician stores the samples below five degrees reads as a description of one person's habit rather than a requirement.
3. So the passive is correct here, and the active version would be a mistake.
Same construction, opposite verdicts, and the question decided both in one step.
grammar.commonMistake: Assuming all passives are evasive and rewriting processes into the active, which produces worse writing and invents people who are not the point. The opposite error is reaching for the passive by default in anything official, so that decisions, refusals and instructions arrive with nobody attached — which is how it has been decided becomes the house style of an organisation.
grammar.memoryTip: Unknown, obvious or irrelevant? Then it is fine. Otherwise, ask who is missing.
grammar.practice:
Write FINE or HIDING, and for each HIDING one, restore the agent.
1. The window was broken overnight.
2. Mistakes were made.
3. Samples are stored below five degrees.
4. Your application has been rejected.
5. The suspect was arrested.
6. It has been decided that the service will be suspended.
7. Every unit must be inspected before dispatch.
8. Staff levels have been reduced.
grammar.answerKey:
1. FINE — unknown.
2. HIDING — somebody made them. Restored: we made mistakes. / The shift manager made two errors.
3. FINE — irrelevant; it is a rule about samples.
4. HIDING — a person or panel rejected it. Restored: The panel has rejected your application.
5. FINE — obvious; by the police.
6. HIDING — twice. Restored: The regional manager has decided to suspend the service.
7. FINE — irrelevant; it is a requirement, not a description of anybody's job.
8. HIDING — somebody reduced them. Restored: We have cut twelve posts.
The four HIDING items all concern a decision, a refusal or a consequence, which is where this use clusters. The four FINE items are a rule, a requirement, an unknown and an obvious agent.
Notice how much number 8 changes when restored: we have cut twelve posts names the actor, the action and the number, and staff levels have been reduced names none of them.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 6 Unit 8; Grade 7 Unit 3, Grade 7 Unit 4, Grade 7 Unit 5; Grade 8 Unit 2, Grade 8 Unit 4
writing.title: Writing 1 — A process, twice
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose a process you know well — a procedure at work, a routine, how something is made, handled or checked.
Write it twice.
Version A: all passive, no people, eight to ten sentences.
Version B: the same process in the active, with people supplied wherever the passive removed one.
Then write three lines: how many people you had to invent for B, which version is easier to follow, and one sentence where the active is genuinely better.
writing.modelText:
Version A:
Deliveries are booked in on arrival and checked against the order. Any damaged items are recorded and set aside. The remainder is allocated to a bay and logged on the system. Pallets are inspected before they are stacked and anything above the marked line is broken down and reloaded. Loading sheets are completed at the end of each shift and countersigned. Sheets that have not been completed are flagged the following morning. Discrepancies are traced to the shift on which they occurred. Anything unresolved after two days is escalated.

Version B:
A warehouse assistant books the deliveries in on arrival and checks them against the order. The assistant records any damaged items and sets them aside. They then allocate the remainder to a bay and log it on the system. A second assistant inspects the pallets before stacking them, and if anything is above the marked line, they break it down and reload it. The shift supervisor completes the loading sheets at the end of each shift and a second supervisor countersigns them. The morning supervisor flags any sheets that have not been completed. The stock controller traces discrepancies to the shift on which they occurred. The shift manager escalates anything unresolved after two days.

1. I had to invent four people: a warehouse assistant, a second assistant, a second supervisor, and a stock controller. None of them is named in the actual procedure.
2. Version A is easier to follow, because the reader tracks one thing — the delivery — through eight steps instead of tracking five people.
3. The last sentence is genuinely better active. Escalation is somebody's responsibility, and anything unresolved after two days is escalated leaves it unclear whose.
writing.successCriteria: Version A eight to ten sentences, all passive, with no people; version B the same process with an agent supplied for every step; three lines counting the invented people, comparing readability, and identifying one sentence where the active genuinely wins
writing.support: Write A first and then convert. Converting forces you to notice how many agents the passive was letting you leave out, which is the finding the exercise is built around.
writing.extension: Look for any step in A where you also could not name the agent even if you wanted to. Those are the steps nobody has actually been assigned.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Restore the agents
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Find a real document that uses the passive heavily — a policy, a decision letter, terms and conditions, a report, an official notice.
Copy out eight passive sentences.
For each, apply the test and write FINE or HIDING.
For every HIDING one, write the restored version with the agent in it.
Then write two lines: which restoration changed the most, and whether you think the original was deliberate or habitual.
writing.modelText:
1. Applications are assessed against the published criteria. — FINE, the process matters more than the assessor.
2. Your application has been unsuccessful on this occasion. — HIDING. Restored: The panel did not shortlist your application.
3. Documents must be submitted by 5pm. — FINE, it is a rule and applies to everyone.
4. It has been determined that you do not meet criterion 3. — HIDING. Restored: The panel decided you do not meet criterion 3.
5. Feedback is not routinely provided. — HIDING. Restored: We do not routinely provide feedback.
6. Late applications will not be considered. — FINE, the rule is what matters.
7. A review of the process is being undertaken. — HIDING. Restored: The department is reviewing the process.
8. This decision is final. — FINE, though it is not really a passive; it just reads like one.

1. Number 5 changed the most. Feedback is not routinely provided sounds like a property of feedback; we do not routinely provide feedback names a choice the organisation has made, and somebody could be asked to change it.
2. I think 2 and 4 are deliberate, because a rejection is exactly where an organisation prefers not to name a decider. I think 5 and 7 are habitual — the register was already established by the time those sentences were written.
writing.expectedLength: Eight sentences with verdicts plus two lines
writing.successCriteria: Eight genuine passive sentences from a real document; a FINE or HIDING verdict for each with the test applied; a restored version for every HIDING one that names a plausible agent; two lines identifying the biggest change and distinguishing deliberate from habitual
writing.support: Look for the pattern first: FINE passives cluster in the sections describing rules and procedures, and HIDING ones cluster wherever a decision, a refusal or a consequence is being reported. Sorting by section before you start makes the pattern visible.
writing.extension: Count the passives in the procedural sections and in the decision sections. The ratio is usually similar; the difference is whether an agent exists.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the findings and the letter
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the findings and letter in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Clause 4.1 keeps a by phrase. Why does it earn its place there?
2. What does clause 4.6 conclude, and does the letter say it?
3. Name three passives in the letter that hide a known agent, and say who each hides.
4. The letter says procedure 7.1 was not followed. What does that sentence let the reader assume?
5. Rewrite the letter so it is accurate to the findings. What has to change?
writing.modelText:
1. Because a findings report has to record who did the inspecting — it is exactly the kind of fact that might be checked or challenged later. Removing it would make the finding unverifiable.
2. It records a breach of procedure 7.1 and attributes responsibility to the shift manager. The letter never mentions the shift manager and never says that Ms Adeyemi was not responsible.
3. It has been found — by the investigation, whose members are named in the findings. It has been decided — by whoever took the decision. This matter is now considered closed — by whoever is closing it. All three agents exist and are known within the organisation.
4. It lets the reader assume the recipient did not follow it. The findings say the opposite: she was allocated to another bay all week and no instruction to cover Bay 2 was issued to her.
5. Model: Dear Ms Adeyemi, We have reviewed loading practice on Bay 2 for the week commencing 9 March. We found that three trolleys were overloaded and that the loading sheet had not been completed. We also found that you were allocated to Bay 3 for that week and that the shift manager did not ask you to cover Bay 2. We have concluded that responsibility rests with the shift manager, not with you. We are issuing a written reminder to all warehouse staff about procedure 7.1. No action is being taken in respect of you and we are closing this matter.
What had to change: every passive that hid a known agent became active, and the finding that exonerates her had to be added — it was missing entirely.
writing.successCriteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 identifies both the conclusion and its absence from the letter; answer 3 names three passives and their agents; answer 4 states what the reader would wrongly assume; answer 5 supplies a letter that names agents and includes the exonerating finding
writing.support: Read the letter alone first, without the findings, and write down what you would believe about your own position if you received it. Then read the findings. The gap between the two is the whole exercise.
writing.extension: The letter contains no untrue sentence. Explain to somebody how a document with no false statements in it can leave its reader with a false belief.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Make it passive
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Make each one passive. Leave the agent out unless it adds something.
1. They check the trolleys.
2. They checked the trolleys on Tuesday.
3. Somebody broke the door.
4. She wrote the report.
5. They inspect every unit before dispatch.

10. Somebody gave the wrong instruction.

1. The trolleys are checked.
2. The trolleys were checked on Tuesday.
3. The door was broken.
4. The report was written.
5. Every unit is inspected before dispatch.
6. The order was dispatched on Tuesday.
7. The wrong file was taken.
8. The new system has been installed.
9. Hazardous materials are stored separately.
10. The wrong instruction was given.
11. The offer was withdrawn.
12. The incident is being investigated.

4. past continuous

With check: 1. are checked  2. was checked  3. is being checked  4. was being checked  5. have been checked  6. had been checked  7. will be checked  8. must be checked  9. should be checked  10. can be checked  11. might have been checked  12. has to be checked  13. has not been checked  14. was not checked  15. will not be checked  16. must not be checked

activities.title: Practice 3 — Person first
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Make each one passive twice: once with the person as subject, once with the thing. Then mark which English prefers.
1. They gave me the form.
2. They told us nothing.
3. They sent her the wrong part.
4. They offered him a different date.
5. They asked me a difficult question.
6. They showed us the new system.
7. They paid her late.
8. They promised us a decision by Friday.
9. They have sent me the wrong invoice.
10. They were offering us a discount.
11. Somebody should have told me.
12. Nobody has shown him the procedure.
activities.answerSummary:
1. I was given the form. / The form was given to me. — PERSON preferred
2. We were told nothing. / Nothing was told to us. — PERSON strongly preferred
3. She was sent the wrong part. / The wrong part was sent to her. — PERSON
4. He was offered a different date. / A different date was offered to him. — PERSON
5. I was asked a difficult question. / A difficult question was asked of me. — PERSON strongly preferred
6. We were shown the new system. / The new system was shown to us. — PERSON
7. She was paid late. — only one version works naturally here
8. We were promised a decision by Friday. / A decision was promised to us by Friday. — PERSON
9. I have been sent the wrong invoice. — PERSON
10. We were being offered a discount. — PERSON
11. I should have been told. — PERSON
12. He has not been shown the procedure. — PERSON
English prefers the person as subject in every one of these. The thing-first versions are grammatical and several sound distinctly odd, particularly 2 and 5.
Note that the thing-first versions all need to before the person. The person-first versions do not.
Numbers 9 to 12 combine this pattern with the perfect, the continuous and a modal, and the mechanism is unchanged.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Fine or hiding?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write FINE or HIDING. For each HIDING one, restore the agent.
1. The window was broken overnight.
2. Mistakes were made.
3. Samples are stored below five degrees.
4. Your application has been rejected.
5. The suspect was arrested.
6. It has been decided that the service will be suspended.
7. Every unit must be inspected before dispatch.
8. Staff levels have been reduced.
9. The road was closed for two days.
10. It was felt that a different approach was needed.
11. Cardboard is recycled separately.
12. Your account has been suspended.
activities.answerSummary:
1. FINE — unknown.
2. HIDING — restored: we made two mistakes.
3. FINE — irrelevant; it is a rule.
4. HIDING — restored: the panel rejected your application.
5. FINE — obvious; by the police.
6. HIDING, twice — restored: the regional manager has decided to suspend the service.
7. FINE — irrelevant; a requirement, not a description of a job.
8. HIDING — restored: we have cut twelve posts.
9. FINE — probably obvious, and if not, unknown to the writer.
10. HIDING — restored: I thought a different approach was needed. This is the worst one in the list, because it hides an opinion as well as a person.
11. FINE — irrelevant; a rule about cardboard.
12. HIDING — restored: we have suspended your account.
The six FINE items are rules, requirements and genuinely unknown agents. The six HIDING items are all decisions, refusals, consequences or opinions — which is exactly where this use clusters.
Number 10 is worth the most attention. It was felt disguises a judgement as a weather event, and there is no version of it that does not have somebody doing the feeling.
Compare 8 and its restoration. Staff levels have been reduced names no actor, no number and no action. We have cut twelve posts names all three.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Count them in a real document
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find one official document — a policy, a decision letter, terms, a report, a notice.
Count the passive constructions on one page.
Sort them into FINE and HIDING using the test.
Then note where each group appears: which sections are full of FINE passives, and which are full of HIDING ones.
Write one line on what the distribution tells you.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your document.
What most people find: the passives are not evenly spread. Procedural sections — how something is done, what the rules are — are full of legitimate passives, because those sections genuinely are about processes.
Decision sections are full of the other kind. Anywhere a document reports a refusal, a penalty, a change of terms or a conclusion, the agents disappear.
That distribution is the finding, and it holds across almost every kind of official document. The passive is not the organisation's house style; it is the style of one particular kind of sentence, and that kind is always the one where somebody made a choice.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Rewrite one you received
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find a letter or message you have received from an organisation that uses the passive to avoid naming anybody.
Rewrite it with every known agent restored.
Then write two lines: what the rewritten version reveals that the original does not, and whether you would send the rewritten version if you worked there.
activities.answerSummary:
No key.
What most people find: the rewritten version is shorter and considerably more uncomfortable to read, because naming an actor makes a decision look like something somebody chose rather than something that happened.
The second finding is the interesting one, and the question is asked deliberately. Most people say they would not send the rewritten version, and the reasons are worth examining — some are good, such as protecting an individual member of staff from being personally blamed for an organisational decision, and some are not, such as making a refusal harder to challenge.
Both reasons produce the same sentence, which is why you cannot tell from the passive alone which one you are looking at. What you can do is notice that a choice was made and ask who made it.

1. The trolleys are checked.
2. The trolleys were checked on Tuesday.
3. The door was broken.
4. The report was written.
5. Every unit is inspected before dispatch.
6. The order was dispatched on Tuesday.
7. The wrong file was taken.
8. The new system has been installed.
9. Hazardous materials are stored separately.
10. The wrong instruction was given.
11. The offer was withdrawn.
12. The incident is being investigated.
The irregular participles here are broken, written, taken, given and withdrawn. Those are where the visible errors happen — was broke, was wrote, was took.
None of the twelve needs a by phrase. In every case the agent is either unknown, obvious or irrelevant, which is the normal situation and the reason the passive exists.
Number 12 needs being, because the investigation is happening now rather than being a standing fact.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
With check: 1. are checked  2. was checked  3. is being checked  4. was being checked  5. have been checked  6. had been checked  7. will be checked  8. must be checked  9. should be checked  10. can be checked  11. might have been checked  12. has to be checked  13. has not been checked  14. was not checked  15. will not be checked  16. must not be checked
With write: are written, was written, is being written, was being written, have been written, had been written, will be written, must be written, should be written, can be written, might have been written, has to be written, has not been written, was not written, will not be written, must not be written.
The participle never changed in either set — checked sixteen times, written sixteen times. Everything that moved was be.
That is the whole point of the mechanism, and doing it twice with a regular and an irregular verb is what makes it visible.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. I was given the form. / The form was given to me. — PERSON preferred
2. We were told nothing. / Nothing was told to us. — PERSON strongly preferred
3. She was sent the wrong part. / The wrong part was sent to her. — PERSON
4. He was offered a different date. / A different date was offered to him. — PERSON
5. I was asked a difficult question. / A difficult question was asked of me. — PERSON strongly preferred
6. We were shown the new system. / The new system was shown to us. — PERSON
7. She was paid late. — only one version works naturally here
8. We were promised a decision by Friday. / A decision was promised to us by Friday. — PERSON
9. I have been sent the wrong invoice. — PERSON
10. We were being offered a discount. — PERSON
11. I should have been told. — PERSON
12. He has not been shown the procedure. — PERSON
English prefers the person as subject in every one of these. The thing-first versions are grammatical and several sound distinctly odd, particularly 2 and 5.
Note that the thing-first versions all need to before the person. The person-first versions do not.
Numbers 9 to 12 combine this pattern with the perfect, the continuous and a modal, and the mechanism is unchanged.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. FINE — unknown.
2. HIDING — restored: we made two mistakes.
3. FINE — irrelevant; it is a rule.
4. HIDING — restored: the panel rejected your application.
5. FINE — obvious; by the police.
6. HIDING, twice — restored: the regional manager has decided to suspend the service.
7. FINE — irrelevant; a requirement, not a description of a job.
8. HIDING — restored: we have cut twelve posts.
9. FINE — probably obvious, and if not, unknown to the writer.
10. HIDING — restored: I thought a different approach was needed. This is the worst one in the list, because it hides an opinion as well as a person.
11. FINE — irrelevant; a rule about cardboard.
12. HIDING — restored: we have suspended your account.
The six FINE items are rules, requirements and genuinely unknown agents. The six HIDING items are all decisions, refusals, consequences or opinions — which is exactly where this use clusters.
Number 10 is worth the most attention. It was felt disguises a judgement as a weather event, and there is no version of it that does not have somebody doing the feeling.
Compare 8 and its restoration. Staff levels have been reduced names no actor, no number and no action. We have cut twelve posts names all three.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key — it is your document.
What most people find: the passives are not evenly spread. Procedural sections — how something is done, what the rules are — are full of legitimate passives, because those sections genuinely are about processes.
Decision sections are full of the other kind. Anywhere a document reports a refusal, a penalty, a change of terms or a conclusion, the agents disappear.
That distribution is the finding, and it holds across almost every kind of official document. The passive is not the organisation's house style; it is the style of one particular kind of sentence, and that kind is always the one where somebody made a choice.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key.
What most people find: the rewritten version is shorter and considerably more uncomfortable to read, because naming an actor makes a decision look like something somebody chose rather than something that happened.
The second finding is the interesting one, and the question is asked deliberately. Most people say they would not send the rewritten version, and the reasons are worth examining — some are good, such as protecting an individual member of staff from being personally blamed for an organisational decision, and some are not, such as making a refusal harder to challenge.
Both reasons produce the same sentence, which is why you cannot tell from the passive alone which one you are looking at. What you can do is notice that a choice was made and ask who made it.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Be plus the past participle — The tense lives in be and the participle never changes, which is why one rule produces ten structures across every tense you already have.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The door was broken overnight. — The passive takes the past participle, not the past simple. With regular verbs the two are identical, so the error only shows with irregular ones.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: About 80 per cent of the time — Most passives exist precisely because the agent is unknown, obvious or beside the point, so naming it would add nothing.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Every unit must be checked before dispatch. — After a modal, be appears in its plain form and never inflects. The participle follows unchanged.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The first is a standing fact; the second is happening now — Being is what makes a passive continuous. Without it, the sentence says the system is in place rather than that work is under way.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I was given the form. — With two-object verbs English prefers the person as subject. Both versions are correct, and the thing-first one needs to before the person.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The thing matters more than the person doing it — Rewriting a process actively forces people into a sentence that was never about people, and the reader then has to track a cast instead of a sequence.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Is the agent unknown, obvious or irrelevant? — Yes to any of the three means the passive is right and often better than the active. No means the agent is known and relevant, and you should ask why they are missing.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: It has been decided that the service will be suspended. — Somebody decided, and who decided is exactly what a reader would want to know. The other three have agents that are unknown, irrelevant or obvious.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Both remove the agent — They travel together, and there has been a reduction in staffing levels does both in eight words — a nominalisation and no person anywhere.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: It removes the person, so the reader assumes it was the recipient — The findings say the shift manager failed to issue an instruction. The letter's sentence is true and leaves the reader with the opposite impression.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Findings must record who did the inspecting, in case it is challenged — That is a by phrase earning its place. It contrasts with the letter, where no agent appears anywhere despite all of them being known.
